source.title: Noise Injection Systemically Degrades Large Language Model Safety Guardrails
source.authors: Prithviraj Singh Shahani; Kaveh Eskandari Miandoab; Matthias Scheutz

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some internal reporting inconsistencies are noted under problems.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites prior work on refusal directions and projection attacks but does not extract, remove, add, or test the difference-in-means refusal direction. Its experiments test Gaussian activation noise, a different intervention, and do not establish that noise suppresses that direction.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-output rates under Gaussian noise and discusses refusal robustness generally. Those results do not test any listed version about the single refusal direction. The cited discussion of direction removal is prior work, not a result of this study. Rows below record the adjacent noise results as findings that fit no listed version.
record.test_reason: The study injects isotropic Gaussian noise into all layer activations and scores harmful outputs with Llama Guard 3 and GPT-OSS. It never extracts, ablates, adds or weight-edits a difference-in-means refusal direction. It cites Arditi et al. only in related work and borrows their harmful-prompt dataset. No result bears on V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude three things. (1) Gaussian activation noise raises harmful-output rates by up to about 30% (p<0.001) across most models, with Qwen2.5 (RL-trained) more resilient. (2) Deeper fine-tuning, tested on GSM8K math accuracy rather than safety, gives only marginal protection, because models converge under high noise. (3) Noise-augmented safety tuning helps only within the training noise range. They call this a systemic brittleness of post-hoc safety fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The study adds random Gaussian noise to activations across layers during inference; it does not extract or project out a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, or add that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported harmful-output rate varies with noise magnitude and model; Qwen2.5 is described as more resilient, and Yi's listed rates decrease under noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Isotropic Gaussian activation noise across all layers raised harmful-output rates on Arditi et al.'s harmful prompts in most of the 9 instruct models. Effects were non-monotonic in some models (Qwen2, Gemma-2 9B) and reversed in Yi 1.5. Qwen2.5 was more resilient.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Untargeted Gaussian activation noise degrades refusal of harmful prompts in many safety-tuned LLMs, with model-dependent magnitude and direction.

record.problems: Experiment A uses 12 trials per model, and the noise ranges were selected after a pilot with n = 1. The authors note that Llama Guard 3 and GPT-OSS may misclassify incoherent outputs as harmful, and that the harmful-prompt dataset lacks ground-truth labels for outputs. The appendix reports a Gemma-2 9B comparison at σ = 1.0 although its table's largest listed value is σ = 0.9; the Qwen 2 appendix comparison names σ = 0.003 although its table lists noise values from 0.020 to 0.0350. The Gemma 2B appendix mean-difference statement is also malformed.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the experiment's intermediate noise levels, Experiment B fine-tuning-depth plots, or Experiment C noise-tuned training were extracted: these do not test a listed refusal-direction version, and the rows retained represent the highest listed noise setting for each Experiment A model. The paper reports Experiment B's convergence under high noise qualitatively in Figure 3 and Experiment C's noise-range results in Figure 4 and the discussion.

untested.parts: No direction is identified, ablated or added. No refusal induction on harmless prompts and no capability preservation under direction removal.
There is no measurement of whether noise or jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction, and no training against direction ablation. Noise-augmented fine-tuning is a different defense.
Harm judgment and refusal are not separated.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct direction transfer.
Training effects are discussed only for noise robustness (Qwen2.5 RL, fine-tuning depth), not for whether a removable direction exists.
The only reasoning-model result is a baseline harmful rate for DeepSeek-R1-distilled Llama 8B, with no direction analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The relation could arguably be uses_without_test, since the study uses Arditi et al.'s harmful-instruction dataset. However, it does not use the refusal-direction finding itself, so cites_only/T6 stands. The Mistral (70%) and DeepSeek-R1-distill Llama 8B (71%) baseline harmful rates are reported in the text but bear on no version. Llama Guard may score incoherent noisy outputs as unsafe, which the authors acknowledge.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is identified, ablated, or added; refusal on harmless requests and preservation of other abilities under direction removal are not tested.
No weight edit or abliteration procedure is evaluated.
The noise attack is not shown to suppress the refusal direction, and training against that direction's ablation is not tested.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account is made.
Harmfulness classification is used to score outputs; the study does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
No transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages is tested.

Fine-tuning depth is studied for mathematical reasoning, and noise-augmented safety training is evaluated as a defense; neither tests whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
Reasoning models and refusal-direction behavior in them are not evaluated; reasoning is suggested as future work.
